title: Symphony No. 4 in F minor
hook: A brass fanfare that Tchaikovsky called Fate, and a symphony that keeps running into it.

painting.title: Shrovetide
painting.pairingNote: Sledges, swings and crowds at a Russian winter fair; the “festive merriment of ordinary people” that Tchaikovsky said his finale pictures.

facts: Tchaikovsky began the symphony in the spring of 1877 and finished it in January 1878 in San Remo. In between, he married in the summer of 1877; by the autumn the marriage had collapsed and he had fled abroad. He completed the scoring in Venice and San Remo, and wrote that no earlier orchestral work had cost him such labour.
The score is dedicated “to my best friend”: Nadezhda von Meck, the wealthy widow who paid him an allowance on condition that they never meet. He called it “our symphony” in his letters to her.

At her request he wrote down a programme. The opening fanfare, he said, is Fate, “the seed of the whole symphony”, a force that stops happiness from reaching its goal. Life is an alternation of hard reality with fleeting dreams of happiness.

Nikolai Rubinstein conducted the first performance in Moscow on 22 February 1878. Tchaikovsky was in Florence. He kept a special love for the work; ten years later he still called it his best symphonic piece.
bigPicture.inOneLine: Fate against dreams in a long, stormy waltz (I), an evening song of memories (II), a scherzo plucked by the strings (III), a folk festival that Fate interrupts (IV).

movements.heading: Andante sostenuto – Moderato con anima
movements.summary: The longest movement, almost as long as the other three together. A brass fanfare opens it and comes back to cut off each section, like a gate slamming shut. Between the fanfares come two kinds of music: a restless, limping waltz in F minor, and softer, dreamlike themes that drift into far-off keys.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfare
mainIdeas.description: horns and bassoons, then trumpets, hammering out one repeated note in a stiff, dotted rhythm. Tchaikovsky’s “Fate”.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a sighing, syncopated melody in the violins that sways in three. The score marks it “in waltz movement”.

mainIdeas.name: The dream themes
mainIdeas.description: a wistful clarinet solo, then a gentle, swaying tune over soft drum rolls.

stops.hear: Horns and bassoons blare a hard, repeated-note call; the trumpets join it higher up
stops.happening: The fanfare, the [[motif|motif]] Tchaikovsky called Fate

stops.hear: Heavy, jolting chords, then two loud strokes separated by silence; the music sinks away
The violins begin a sighing, uneasy tune that seems to limp on its off-beats
stops.happening: Theme 1, *Moderato con anima*, in 9/8: a waltz that cannot settle

stops.hear: The tune is passed through the orchestra and swells to a loud, anxious climax
Very quietly, a solo clarinet plays a wistful, swaying melody; flute and bassoon answer
stops.happening: The dream begins: the second theme, far from home in A-flat minor

stops.hear: A gentle, rocking tune in the strings over soft timpani rolls; it brightens and grows into a broad, happy climax
stops.happening: The dream of happiness, in B major

stops.hear: The trumpets crash in with the fanfare
stops.happening: Fate wakes the dreamer. The [[development|development]] begins

stops.hear: The fanfare in the brass and the waltz tune in the strings collide at full force
The opening tune returns, loud and grim, in the whole orchestra
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]], not in F minor but in D minor

stops.hear: The fanfare again
Faster and faster; the waltz tune is driven to a furious end in F minor

notice: Count the fanfares. Each one ends a section: listen for the moment it breaks into the dream music.
Try to tap the waltz in Theme 1. The accents keep landing between the beats, which is why it never feels like a dance you could actually dance.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Antonio Pappano became music director of the orchestra of Rome’s Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia in 2005. This performance was recorded live at concerts in the orchestra’s hall, the Sala Santa Cecilia, in July 2006, together with the Fifth and Sixth; EMI issued the three in 2007. On the Spotify album the Fourth is tracks 1–4.

movements.heading: Andantino in modo di canzona
movements.summary: A slow song, as the title says. Tchaikovsky described it as the melancholy of evening, when you sit alone with a book that falls from your hand and memories crowd in. The oboe’s tune frames the movement; a livelier middle section rises to a loud climax, and then the tune returns, decorated, and fades.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a plain, sad melody for solo oboe over plucked strings.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: a firmer, dance-like tune that builds up energy.

stops.hear: A few soft plucked notes, then a solo oboe sings a slow, sad tune
stops.happening: The main theme, in B-flat minor

stops.hear: The cellos take the tune, darker and warmer
stops.happening: The song repeated in a new colour

stops.hear: The strings spin out a gentler, more hopeful phrase, then the sad tune returns
stops.happening: A contrasting idea, and the song again

stops.hear: Faster: a sturdy, dance-like tune that swells to a loud climax with the brass
stops.happening: The middle section (*Più mosso*), in F major

stops.hear: The violins play the oboe’s tune; woodwinds weave quick decorations around it

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music thins out; a bassoon plays the last phrase alone and the movement fades

notice: Compare the oboe and the cellos in the first two minutes: the same tune, two colours.
When the tune returns after the climax, listen to the flutes and clarinets around it. Tchaikovsky’s memories come back blurred and decorated.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Pizzicato ostinato – Allegro
movements.summary: The strings put away their bows and pluck the whole movement. Tchaikovsky wrote that this was a new orchestral effect he had designed himself. Woodwinds and brass get their own sections, and at the end the three groups toss the music between them. Tchaikovsky’s picture: idle fancies after a little wine, a drunken peasant song, a military band passing in the distance.

mainIdeas.name: The woodwinds
mainIdeas.description: a jaunty, rustic tune, like a village band.

mainIdeas.name: The brass
mainIdeas.description: a tiny, distant march, very quiet and clipped.

stops.hear: Only plucked strings: a quick, light tune that rises and falls in waves
The plucking grows louder and swirls through the whole string section
An oboe holds a long high note; then the woodwinds play a jaunty tune
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]], in A major: the peasant song

stops.hear: Brass alone, very quiet and short-noted, like a band marching far away
The plucked strings return
Strings, woodwinds and brass throw short scraps of their tunes to each other

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A few soft plucked notes, and silence

notice: The three groups never play the same tune together: listen for how they hand the music on.
The only percussion in this movement is the timpani. Everything else that sounds like a drum is plucked strings.

movements.heading: Finale: Allegro con fuoco
movements.summary: A crash of cymbals and rushing scales, and the finale is a folk festival. Tchaikovsky’s advice: if you find no joy in yourself, go out among the people. In the middle of the celebration the Fate fanfare from the first movement returns. Then the crowd sweeps the lonely listener back into the fun.

mainIdeas.name: The festival
mainIdeas.description: loud, rushing scales and chords for the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The folk song
mainIdeas.description: a small, plaintive tune, “In the Field a Birch Tree Stood”, that is repeated over and over in changing colours.
The fanfare from the first movement.

stops.hear: A cymbal crash and rushing scales from the whole orchestra
The woodwinds play a short, sad little tune, quietly
stops.happening: The folk song “In the Field a Birch Tree Stood”, in A minor

stops.hear: The rushing scales return
A bright, marching tune with cymbals
The folk song keeps coming back, louder, in new keys and new instruments, with a busy accompaniment
stops.happening: The folk song as a set of [[variation|variation]]s

stops.hear: The trumpets blast the fanfare from the first movement; two crashing chords and silence
Quietly, the folk song returns, then the festival music picks itself up again

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: Ever faster and louder, ending in F major with crashing chords

notice: Follow the folk song: it is only a few notes long, but it is heard many times, each time dressed differently.
When the fanfare returns, notice that it no longer has the last word: the festival does.

threads.title: Fate
threads.body: The opening fanfare returns in the first movement as a structural marker and once in the finale. Tchaikovsky told a friend that the symphony’s central idea mirrored Beethoven’s Fifth.

threads.title: Dreams and reality
threads.body: In the first movement the dream themes are always broken off. The finale finds a different answer: joy in other people.

threads.title: Colour as structure
threads.body: Tchaikovsky separates the orchestra into groups: strings, woodwinds and brass each have their own territory in the scherzo, and the fanfare is always brass.

threads.title: A symphony with a story
threads.body: Tchaikovsky wrote the programme for von Meck, but warned her that music does not yield to detailed explanation. The story is a way in, not a map.
